results.title: The Cloud GPU Glut Nobody Wants to Admit | MarketIntel
highlights:
Consider the specific unit economics reported by Lambda Labs. The company disclosed in its Q1 2026 update that its H100 spot pricing had fallen to $2.10 per hour, representing a massive drop from a peak of $4.80 in mid-2024. That is a fifty-six percent decline in just twenty months, and the critical detail is that Lambda remains profitable on that reduced pricing. The implication of this profitability is deeply uncomfortable for the structural shortage thesis. If a second-tier provider can clear its hardware and operational costs at $2.10 per hour, the marginal cost of enterprise GPU compute is falling rapidly. Consequently, the scarcity premium that hyperscalers have embedded into their long-term contracts is evaporating right in front of the market's eyes.

...

The consensus models are misreading four distinct signals that point directly to this market bifurcation. The first signal emerges from the secondary market for H100 hardware. Major cloud providers and colocation operators are now offering H100 capacity at rates that imply a hardware depreciation curve significantly steeper than the one most financial analysts currently model. H100 spot pricing on secondary platforms like Vast.ai and RunPod has consistently hovered between $1.80 and $2.40 per hour through the first half of 2026, according to publicly tracked indices. This pricing behavior shows that the marginal H100, once it leaves the pristine environment of a hyperscaler's primary contract, earns roughly half of what it commanded at peak demand. The depreciation is not just real; it is accelerating as more chips enter the secondary pool and compete for the same enterprise workloads.

results.title: GPU Rentals Are Up, Not Down: The 'Glut' Crowd Is Reading the Wrong Price | AInvest
highlights:
- Claims of 60-75% GPU rental price drops rely on 2024 peak comparisons, ignoring 2026's 40% H100 contract price rise.

...

Every few weeks, someone in the AI supply chain repeats the same figure: GPU rental prices are down 60-75% from their peak, therefore the AI buildout is cresting, therefore the bears are vindicated. In late August 2026 that claim is circulating again, and it is propaganda dressed as a price signal. The number is technically correct against a single baseline — late 2024 — and useless for the question everyone is actually asking. There is no such thing as the GPU rental price. There are at least three markets: long-term committed contracts, on-demand reserved instances, and interruptible spot capacity. Right now they are moving in different directions. Anyone quoting one number for the whole system is selecting a narrative, not reporting a market.

...

Start with the tier that clears real committed demand: one-year H100 rental contracts. The SemiAnalysis index put these at a low of $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 and up almost 40% to $2.35 an hour in March. The spot market went from "finally cooling off" in October to a hard squeeze again in roughly five months. The famous "GPU glut" of 2025 did not survive contact with the 2026 order book.

The on-demand readings tell the same story in miniature. Silicon Data's daily H100 neo-cloud index — a standardized hourly rate across cloud providers — went from $2.57 in early May to $2.75 by late July, while the H200 climbed from $2.70 to $3.09, a 14.4% rise, with the H200's premium over the H100 peaking above 16%. Through mid-summer 2026, the load-bearing tiers of the rental market were up, or flat-to-slightly-up. Not collapsing.

So where does the "down 64-75%" claim come from? It is a comparison against the 2024 peak of $8-10 an hour — a generation-specific high-water mark set when the whole market was fighting over a pre-Blackwell chip in a finance-driven frenzy. That baseline tells you H100s were overpriced in 2024, not that AI demand is falling in 2026. Using a bubble peak as the demand benchmark is the analytical equivalent of calling the whole equity market a bubble because the 2021 meme stocks never came back.

...

Now the tier the collapse stories actually live in: spot. The survey data is a carnival. One tracker covering 52 clouds puts the H100 on-demand average at $4.08 an hour, the low at $1.73, and spot instances as low as $0.45. On AWS, H100 spot swung from $2.10 to $14.80 within a single week in April. That 7x range is not a malfunction; it is the structural condition of a spot market that clears whatever capacity nobody wants, whenever nobody wants it.

...

The demand-leading indicator is next-generation pricing, and it is bending the wrong way for the bears. Across the providers compiled into one industry GPU index, on-demand rates for the newest parts — B200, B300, MI300X — roughly doubled over the past year, while the mainstream H100, H200 and A100 band held tight. A market whose demand was cresting would not price its scarcest compute at double the prior year's level. Scarcity has migrated from H100 to H200 to Blackwell, and the direction of that migration is the demand story: up.

results.title: The sovereign cloud is repricing. It isn't regulation, it's RAM.
highlights:
OVHcloud, in August: dedicated servers repriced for new orders, memory and storage options from 1 July and whole configurations from 11 August — the 2026 game servers up 74% and 100%, 87% on average; other 2026 configurations up to 83%, 2024 ones up to 49%. A running server takes the new rate at its first renewal from 1 October, its installed RAM rising three to six times less than the same module ordered new, and its storage less again. On Public Cloud, the 1‑, 6‑ and 24‑month Savings Plans went on 1 September, leaving 12 and 36, and since 1 October local storage and the IPv4 address have had their own meters. The cause, in OVHcloud’s words: memory costs six times what it did a year ago. Octave Klaba went further on X, as The Register reported it: RAM ×9 forecast by September and ×12 for 2027; NVMe ×7; disks ×3.5. His line was not about price: “the real risk is not being able to fulfill your orders.” He hopes for normal in 2029.

Hetzner has done it twice: up to 37% on 1 April, on existing products as well as new orders, then every dedicated server and cloud plan on 15 June — a CPX22 from €7.99 to €19.49 a month, a CCX13 from €15.99 to €42.99, both excluding the €0.50 IPv4 — this time for new orders and rescales only; servers already rented kept their price.

AWS has raised one list price this year that I can find: EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, the reserved GPU blocks, about 15% in January and about 20% in July — on supply and demand, AWS says. General‑purpose EC2 has not moved, and AWS said, as TNW reports, that its other purchase options keep fixed prices. That it moves later anyway is my expectation, not an announcement.

The providers that rent you the box have repriced it. General-purpose EC2 has not; that it will is my expectation, not AWS's.

...

- Renewal vs new order. OVH reprices a running server at renewal, but far less than a new one: an ADVANCE‑1 Gen 2024 with 128 GB of RAM goes up 21.5% at renewal against 72.1% as a new order. Hetzner raised existing servers in April, then spared them in June and repriced rescales as new orders.

...

- The Register, 11 Aug 2026 — OVH Cloud warns of 87% price hikes to help it cover RAMpocalypse costs — Klaba’s component figures and outlook, from his post on X.
- wz‑it — Hetzner price increase June 2026: CPX and CCX up to +176% — before/after prices, the April round’s “up to 37%”.
- TNW — AWS raises GPU prices 20% as the memory crunch bites — Capacity Blocks, January and July.

results.title: H100 Rents Recovered 40% Off the Trough — It's a Depreciation Cycle, Not an AI Boom | AInvest
highlights:
The most quoted price in AI right now is also the least understood: the H100 rental rate. In 2025 the FinTwit headline was "GPU rentals collapsed to $2 an hour — the bubble is bursting." In 2026 the headline flipped to "H100 rents up 40 percent — the boom is back." Both headlines leaned on the same instrument as their sole evidence, and both were wrong for the same reason: an H100 rental quote no longer measures what AI demand is doing. It measures what is left in a three-year-old chip after the market has rotated toward Blackwell.

As of the end of August, the state of the trade is this: the recovery that started late last year is intact, not faded. One-year H100 contracts — the pricing tier that actually clears the market — have climbed roughly 40 percent off the October 2025 trough of $1.70 an hour to $2.35 by March, and current listings still show the median on-demand rate near $3.38 with on-demand inventory sold out through the summer. Investors who shorted the GPU-cloud complex on the 2025 "rental collapse" have been watching the falsifying data accumulate for nine months.

...

The number that matters is the one-year contract, the price a serious tenant signs for twelve months of capacity. That is where the majority of volume transacts, because AI labs and inference operators cannot build a business on spot capacity that can be revoked. On-demand and spot are the residual market — the spillover that happens to be available this hour. This is the same trap we keep flagging in this corner of the market: quoting the smallest, most volatile slice of a market as if it were the market.

...

The recovery is a supply squeeze on a shrunken pool of old chips, driven by four forces that have nothing to do with marginal AI demand being proven. TSMC's CoWoS advanced-packaging capacity — the scarce step that all AI accelerators compete for — was redirected to Blackwell, so virtually no new Hopper capacity is being built. Blackwell itself is rolling out slowly because B200/B300-class systems need liquid cooling and power densities most data centers cannot support without retrofit. Memory prices are inflating replacement cost, with HBM and DRAM contract prices guided up roughly 20 percent for 2026. And the demand that remains is relatively inelastic — agentic and inference workloads pay up regardless of price. NVIDIA NVDA-- has itself been guiding rental prices up about 20 percent for 2026.

The result is 40 percent on one-year contracts and capacity booked out past September. But this is not a broad compute boom, and anyone treating it as one is about to get hurt. A B200 rents for $7 an hour on average against the H100's roughly $3.38 on-demand, and the Blackwell part is up to 57 percent faster at training. When CoWoS capacity normalizes and the Blackwell wave lands in force, the Hopper residual-value party ends. The recovery has a shelf life set by TSMC's packaging ramp, not by AI demand. This is why the H100 index has stopped being an AI-demand meter and become a residual-value meter for a depreciating asset.

results.title: Best GPU Cloud Providers for AI Workloads in 2026: CoreWeave vs Lambda vs RunPod | DevToolLab Blog
highlights:
The pricing spread is wider down here. As of August 22, 2026, an H100 rents for $2.69/hr on RunPod's Community Cloud, $3.29 on its Secure Cloud, $3.99 on Lambda, and $6.16 on CoreWeave on demand, all read from the vendors' pages the day this was written. Then spot inverts the whole table: CoreWeave's 8x H100 node drops from $49.24/hr to $19.71 on spot, which is $2.46 per GPU, cheaper than anyone's on-demand rate. The companies are as unalike as the prices: CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 and reported $5.13 billion in 2025 revenue, Lambda is reportedly on an IPO track for late 2026, and RunPod raised $100 million at a $1 billion valuation in June after turning down buyouts.

...

| Provider | H100 per GPU-hr | Billing | Shape | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RunPod | $2.69 community, $3.29 secure | Per second | Pods, serverless, clusters | Cheapest self-serve GPUs, bursty jobs |
| Lambda | $3.99 on-demand | Self-serve instances | VMs and 1-Click Clusters to 2,000+ GPUs | Straightforward training boxes |
| CoreWeave | $6.16 on-demand, $2.46 spot | Per-instance (8 GPUs) | Kubernetes-native fleets | Reserved scale, newest silicon |
| SkyPilot | Your cheapest cloud | Apache 2.0, 10,518 stars | Orchestrator across all of them | Chasing the lowest price automatically |

One trap before the details: normalize everything to price per GPU-hour. CoreWeave lists $49.24 for an HGX H100, which is an 8-GPU node ($6.16 per GPU, a figure its own table confirms in the single-GPU column), and its GB200 NVL72 instance at $42.00 is 4 GPUs ($10.50 each). Lambda and RunPod list per-GPU prices directly. Comparing a node price to a GPU price is the classic way this shopping trip goes wrong.

...

CoreWeave North America pricing table showing per-instance on-demand, spot, and single-GPU hourly prices: HGX H100 at $49.24 on demand, $19.71 spot, and $6.16 per GPU, HGX B200 at $68.80, GB200 NVL72 at $42.00, and A100 rows below

...

The platform is Kubernetes-native: you get managed clusters and node pools rather than a simple VM picker, which is exactly right for fleets and exactly wrong for a weekend fine-tune. On-demand North America prices per 8-GPU instance: HGX H100 $49.24/hr, HGX H200 $50.44, HGX B200 $68.80, A100 $21.60, with GB300 and B300 behind contact-sales walls. The interesting column is spot: the HGX H100 falls to $19.71/hr ($2.46 per GPU) and the B200 to $34.11 ($4.26 per GPU), undercutting every on-demand price in this post if your training job checkpoints well enough to tolerate preemption.

...

Lambda instances pricing table on the 8x tab showing per-GPU hourly prices: B200 SXM6 at $6.69, H100 SXM at $3.99, A100 SXM 80GB at $2.79, A100 SXM 40GB at $1.99, and Tesla V100 at $0.79, with a sales tax footnote

Lambda sells the simplest mental model of the three: pick an instance, get a price per GPU-hour, plus applicable sales tax. On-demand 8x instances run $3.99 per H100 SXM, $2.79 per A100 80GB, $1.99 per A100 40GB, $6.69 per B200 SXM6, and a nostalgic $0.79 per V100. Above self-serve sit 1-Click Clusters, production blocks of 16 to 2,000+ B200 or H100 GPUs on two-week to one-year terms: 16 B200s cost $9.86 per GPU-hour, dropping to $8.87 at 256+ GPUs.

...

RunPod pods pricing grid showing Secure Cloud hourly prices per GPU: H200 at $4.59, B200 at $6.79, H100 NVL at $3.19, H100 PCIe at $2.89, H100 SXM at $3.29, A100 PCIe at $1.39, A100 SXM at $1.59, and L40S at $0.99

RunPod is the developer cloud of the three, and the only one with a two-tier market. Secure Cloud runs in vetted data centers: H100 SXM $3.29/hr, H100 PCIe $2.89, A100 SXM $1.59, H200 $4.59, B200 $6.79, L40S $0.99. Community Cloud runs on vetted third-party hosts and is the cheapest H100 in this post: we toggled the pricing page ourselves and watched the H100 SXM drop to $2.69 and an RTX 4090 fall from $0.74 to $0.34. Pods are billed by the second, and RunPod's docs add a line the big clouds would never write: no fees for data ingress or egress.

...

An 8x H100 node for a 730-hour month: RunPod Secure $19,214, Lambda $23,302, CoreWeave on-demand $35,945, CoreWeave spot $14,388. The most expensive on-demand provider is the cheapest of all on spot, which is the single most useful fact in this market. For a two-week fine-tune that checkpoints every 30 minutes, spot plus SkyPilot-style auto-recovery is close to free money; for a customer-facing endpoint, it is an outage generator.

Down a tier, the A100 80GB tells the value story: $1.39 to $1.59 on RunPod and $2.79 on Lambda buys a GPU that still fine-tunes 7B and 13B models happily (size your job with our VRAM guide) at a third of H100 pricing. The same normalization exposes the widest relative gap in this post: an L40S is $0.99/hr on RunPod and $2.25 per GPU on CoreWeave, a 2.3x difference on identical hardware. And workload shape changes the winner again, since CoreWeave's single GH200 at $6.50 exists for memory-bound jobs no L40S can hold.

What none of these prices include is worth a sentence: storage and data transfer. RunPod's docs commit to zero ingress and egress fees, Lambda's footnote adds sales tax, and every provider meters persistent storage separately, so a training pipeline that shuttles terabytes should price the disks, not just the silicon.

...

Three habits make this market navigable. Normalize every quote to price per GPU-hour, because node pricing and GPU pricing are deliberately easy to confuse. Ask what the spot or interruptible tier costs, because the most expensive on-demand provider here is also the cheapest source of H100s once preemption is on the table. And check storage and egress before you park a dataset next to the GPUs.

results.title: Nvidia Customers Notified About AI-Related Price Hikes Above 15% - Bloomberg
highlights:
Some of Nvidia Corp.’s biggest customers have been told that the prices of servers containing its artificial intelligence chips are going up more than 15% in many cases with memory chip costs soaring.

The price hikes will go into effect on systems shipped early next year and will impact systems including those with the flagship Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell chips, according to people familiar with the process, who asked to not to be identified commenting on communications that haven’t yet been made public. The increases will depend on the generation of Nvidia chips and the memory configurations, they said.

results.title: Nvidia's Stock Performance: What's Next for AI Chip Prices? (2026)
highlights:
## The Compute Price Decline

One of the key factors behind Nvidia's struggles is the decline in the compute price for its B200 chip. The B200 is Nvidia's flagship GPU, used to run data centers at a massive scale. The compute price for this chip has been on a downward trend, with the price per hour dropping from $6.11 on May 30 to $4.22 as of June 21. This decline in compute price is a significant development, as it could impact Nvidia's ability to generate revenue from its AI chips.

...

Kalshi traders, who are known for their pessimistic outlook on Nvidia's AI chip's compute price, have played a significant role in this development. These traders predict that the compute price for Nvidia's AI chips will not surpass the high reached in May. This prediction is based on the fact that most companies rent access to GPUs through cloud providers or neoclouds, and the cost to rent GPUs can fluctuate as demand for AI infrastructure grows.
